items.title: Agents are sessions, not requests: size GKE node pools for AI agent sessions
items.summary: AI agent sessions remain active and idle for most of the workday, making traditional one-Pod-per-session allocations inefficient for cluster resources. By using open-source tools like Agent Substrate and AX on GKE, developers can park idle sessions in object storage to release compute resources while maintaining session state. This approach optimizes resource utilization and reduces Kubernetes node costs by up to 40%.

items.title: Distributed LLM Training Across Metros: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText
items.summary: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText enables developers to efficiently train large language models across geographically distributed TPU slices by streaming parameter fragments instead of synchronizing full models at every step. This approach slashes cross-slice communication volume by over 60× and eliminates network stalls, allowing seamless multi-datacenter scaling without degrading model convergence or quality.

items.title: On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery
items.summary: Google AI Edge Gallery now supports on-device, offline Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) capabilities for building developer-friendly voice applications. Developers can leverage ML Kit for optimized Android performance, or use MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT for cross-platform open-weight model integration. This local pipeline seamlessly pairs lightweight speech models with on-device small language models like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 to enable real-time streaming transcription and low-latency synthesis.

items.title: Accelerating development for massive Git repositories
items.summary: Meet Another Build File Service (ABFS), Google's open-source content-addressable filesystem and build cache that cuts Android checkouts to <8s and builds to ~2m.

items.title: Check what your AI agents do before they do it, with Semantic governance policies
items.summary: Semantic governance policies enable developers to govern AI agents by evaluating every proposed tool call inline before execution. Operating via Agent Gateway, the policy engine checks each action against user intent and plain-language rules to prevent unauthorized data sharing and prompt injection attacks. Developers can easily attach natural-language constraints to their agents and monitor auditable verdicts through Cloud Logging.

items.title: Catch Go bugs that fuzzing misses with Gemini and a constraint solver
items.summary: How pairing Go's surviving compiler bounds-check traps with Gemini 4 Argon and the Z3 constraint solver catches latent out-of-bounds panics in Go code and uncovers a slice-capacity blind spot in go test -fuzz.

items.title: From Files to Cited Answers in One API Call: Managed Ingestion and SearchDocuments in Agent Retrieval
items.summary: Agent Retrieval in Vertex AI introduces managed ingestion and SearchDocuments to replace custom chunking and embedding pipelines. Developers can now import document and video files directly from Cloud Storage and query them with a single API call for cited page numbers and timestamped results. The feature supports hybrid retrieval, metadata filtering, reranking, and multimodal video audio search.

items.title: Did the user ask for this? Securing AI agents against intent hijacking with Semantic governance policies
items.summary: Semantic governance policies protect AI agents from indirect prompt injection and intent hijacking by validating every proposed tool call against user intent and natural language constraints before execution. As demonstrated on the AgentDojo benchmark using a Gemini 2.5 Flash agent, this mechanism reduced attack success rates from 48.7% to 0.9% while maintaining high task utility. Developers can leverage these policies in preview within the Gemini platform via Agent Gateway to secure tool-use workflows.

items.title: Agent Anomaly Detection: Safeguarding agents across other clouds
items.summary: Agent Anomaly Detection now monitors ADK agents running across AWS, Azure, or on-premises by analyzing their traces and logs in your Google Cloud project. By ingesting OpenTelemetry-formatted data through the Telemetry API, it evaluates full conversations for behavioral drift without needing access to the agent's underlying runtime. This enables security teams to detect risks like rogue behaviors, tool misuse, and resource exhaustion across multi-cloud environments.

items.title: How to handle user, connector, and agent auth in Gemini Enterprise with a custom UI
items.summary: When building a custom enterprise UI on top of Gemini Enterprise's :streamAssist API, developers must manually implement three core authentication layers. These include authenticating users or workloads via Google Identity or Workforce/Workload Identity Federation, managing third-party 3-legged OAuth (3LO) for Federated Connectors through the Keystore, and configuring on-demand per-tool OAuth for custom ADK agents using Vertex AI Agent Engine and GCP Auth Manager.

items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
items.summary: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.

items.title: How to securely connect internal Cloud Run MCP servers to Gemini Enterprise
items.summary: How to connect Gemini Enterprise privately to internal StreamableHTTP MCP servers on Cloud Run using Egress Agent Gateway, Private Service Connect, FQDN-scoped Private Cloud DNS, and dual-header OAuth 2.0 authentication.

items.title: Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Tunix and Gemma 4 on Google TPUs
items.summary: This post walks developers through training a multi-turn, tool-using LLM agent using Tunix and Gemma 4 on Cloud TPUs. By leveraging agentic Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and asynchronous vLLM rollouts, the approach significantly improves complex reasoning and tool compliance in interactive environments.

items.title: Gemini 4 Hydrogen: a faster model for general purpose robotics
items.summary: Google's Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings strong spatial and embodied reasoning capabilities to a fast, efficient model built specifically for robotics. To help developers put these capabilities to work, the new Robotics plugin for Google Antigravity transforms the platform into a comprehensive workbench supporting rapid hardware bring-up, MuJoCo simulation, and closed-loop control. Developers can leverage these tools to transition from an unboxed robot arm to a fully functional real-to-sim-to-real application in an afternoon using natural language prompts and day-one support in the google-genai SDKs.

items.title: A2UI 1.0: Build delightful, fast, reliable, agentic experiences
items.summary: A2UI 1.0 is an open protocol for generative UI that enables AI agents to render interactive, native screens across web, mobile, and desktop applications. Developers can leverage open-source renderer SDKs—including React, Angular, Lit, Flutter, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose—alongside agent SDKs for Python, TypeScript, and Dart. The release introduces bidirectional function calls, swappable inference formats, and secure data binding to help teams seamlessly integrate generative UI into their product stacks.

items.title: TPU Model Design Considerations and Optimization Guide
items.summary: The newly launched AI-Hypercomputer/tpu-codesign guide provides hardware-grounded design rules to help developers maximize performance on TPUs for LLMs and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) workloads. Key principles include aligning reduction and output dimensions to 256 for systolic arrays, adopting LatentMoE to compress routed token traffic, and mapping parallel axes directly onto physical links.

items.title: Unlocking Stable On-Policy RL on TPU with Bitwise-Zero Train–Inference Mismatch
items.summary: How we eliminated floating-point train–inference logprob drift for on-policy LLM reinforcement learning across 64 Cloud TPU v5p chips using a generalizable four-part JAX and Pallas recipe in Tunix.

items.title: Build full-stack Android apps with Gemini in Google AI Studio
items.summary: Google AI Studio now lets developers build, test, and ship full-stack Kotlin Android apps from a single prompt—complete with Cloud Firestore, Firebase Authentication, Firebase AI Logic, a faster HD emulator with audio, visual screenshot debugging, and direct publishing to your personal Google Play library.

items.title: How Agent Anomaly Detection scores on benchmarks we didn't write
items.summary: Agent Anomaly Detection (AAD) provides asynchronous, low-latency monitoring for AI agents by analyzing OpenTelemetry traces and logs to flag goal hijacks and tool misuse. Tested across five public security benchmarks, AAD successfully caught 87% of harmful instructions carried out by agents without adding runtime latency. Developers can integrate AAD alongside semantic governance and strict tool limits as part of a defense-in-depth strategy to secure agentic applications.

items.title: Securing Your Agents: A Hands-On Guide to Agent Anomaly Detection
items.summary: This guide walks developers through setting up Agent Anomaly Detection on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform to monitor AI agent telemetry and catch behavioral risks. It demonstrates how to deploy a sample customer support agent, trigger out-of-scope security findings, and configure proactive alerts using Cloud Monitoring and Security Command Center.

items.title: 1Password Breach Leaked Customer Names and Emails, But Passwords Are Safe
items.summary: Password manager 1Password has confirmed that hackers breached its internal systems on November 19 after gaining access to an employee's corporate GitHub account and pushing malicious code to company servers. The attacker stole customer names, email addresses, account creation dates and last login timestamps, but 1Password said customer password vaults were "at no point" accessible to the attacker and that its apps and browser extensions remain unaffected. TechCrunch reports: It's unclear how the attacker gained access to the employee's corporate account, and a spokesperson for 1Password did not immediately respond to TechCrunch's questions about the incident. 1Password did not say whether it had notified customers whose information was taken in the breach, or how many customers had information taken. [...] The company touts millions of customers and more than 200,000 businesses who use its password manager products to store their passwords, credentials, payment card information, and more. Security experts have long recommended password managers as a better way of generating stronger credentials and keeping track of online accounts. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: 5 production-only bugs I hit shipping my first Android app as a solo founder
items.summary: I'm Mahmood, a solo founder from Pakistan. Last month I shipped Duvello AI, a bill reminder app for Android: you snap a paper bill (or paste the bill SMS), AI fills in the biller, amount and due date, and the app reminds you before every due date. It works offline and in 6 languages. The stack is boring on purpose: React + Vite for the UI Capacitor to wrap it as a native Android app Firebase (Auth, Firestore, Cloud Functions, Crashlytics, Hosting) Google Play Billing for Premium Everything worked perfectly in debug builds on my own phone. Then I shipped, and five bugs showed up that only existed in production. If you're about to ship a Capacitor or React Native app, I hope this saves you a few nights. My Settings screen crashed instantly in the Play Store build. In debug it was fine. The cause: minifyEnabled true turns on R8, which strips classes it thinks are unused. Capacitor finds native plugins by reflection, so R8 had no idea the Google Sign-In plugin class was needed and removed it. The fix was explicit keep rules in proguard-rules.pro: -keep class com.getcapacitor.** { *; } -keep class com.codetrixstudio.capacitor.GoogleAuth.** { *; } -keep class com.google.firebase.** { *;

items.title: JNet in 2026: the JVM and .NET, side by side — three years later
items.summary: Photo by Timo Volz on Unsplash This is a follow-up to Java APIs written in C# — JVM and .NET side by side. If you are new to JNet, start there. Three years ago I wrote about JNet — a project that runs a real JVM inside your .NET process and exposes its entire API surface to C#. The core idea has not changed: no byte-code conversion, no TCP channel, no intermediate layer. One process, two runtimes, one boundary. What has changed is everything around that boundary: how fast it is, how much control you have over it, and what you can do with bulk data crossing it. This article covers what is new. When the first article was published, JNet was essentially a library and a code generator. Today it is the foundation of a larger suite: JNet — the core library. Almost the full Java API surface, plus any JVM language through JNetReflector. JNetReflector — points at any JAR and produces production-ready C# classes. In 2023 it was still maturing; today it generates everything: generics, nested types, default and static interface methods, listener wiring, Dispose patterns. items.summary: If a marketing dashboard reports a lead whenever somebody presses Submit, it probably reports attempts rather than accepted enquiries. Validation errors, blocked requests and double clicks are common, and they are easy to overlook in a tag-only implementation. A data-layer contract gives your website, Google Tag Manager and analytics team one agreed definition of an event. It also prevents every new plugin from becoming an accidental second source of truth. window.dataLayer is a JavaScript array of messages read by tools such as Google Tag Manager. It can carry values and events. It is not a database, an access-controlled vault or proof that a payment went through. The interface should specify what happened, when it happened and the exact non-sensitive properties that are safe to send to measurement destinations. A basic implementation looks like this: window.dataLayer = window.dataLayer || []; window.dataLayer.push({ event: 'course_interest', course: { id: 'digital_marketing', format: 'classroom' }, page_section: 'syllabus' }); In GTM, a Version 2 Data Layer Variable with name course.id reads the nested value. items.title: Modeling Japan's 10 Regional Tiered Electricity Tariffs in a Zero-Backend Web App
items.summary: When building a consumer utility calculator for Japan, a common shortcut is multiplying wattage by the national guideline rate (31 JPY/kWh). In practice, actual household electricity bills vary by up to 1.8x depending on the regional utility, consumption tier, and contract structure. While building 電気代シミュレーターJP (denkidaikeisan.com), I wanted to model all 10 major Japanese electric power companies in a 100% client-side, zero-backend Astro web app. Here is how the tariff math and architecture work. Japan's 10 regional utilities fall into two distinct residential tariff structures: 従量電灯B (Ampere-based, 6 utilities): Hokkaido, Tohoku, Tokyo (TEPCO), Hokuriku, Chubu, and Kyushu. The fixed base fee scales with the contracted breaker capacity (e.g., 30A, 40A, 50A), and every kWh is billed across three progressive tiers (typically 0–120 kWh, 120–300 kWh, and 300+ kWh). 従量電灯A (Minimum-charge, 4 utilities): Kansai, Chugoku, Shikoku, and Okinawa. Instead of an ampere-based base fee, a flat minimum charge covers the first 10–15 kWh, followed by three progressive kWh tiers. items.title: Still on Swagger 2.0? Catch breaking changes without migrating first
items.summary: Somewhere in your company there is a service that still publishes Swagger 2.0. Maybe it's an ASP.NET Core API that set Swashbuckle to 2.0 years ago for an old client. Maybe it's a Spring service on Springfox, or a Go service documented with swag. It works, nobody wants to touch it, and moving it to OpenAPI 3 sits somewhere near the bottom of the backlog. That's fine. A 2.0 spec describes the API just as well, and you can catch the changes in it that break other teams without migrating anything first. We build Graphwake, which tells the teams that consume an API when a change in its spec is about to break them. Graphwake doesn't read your code; it works only from the spec and from the endpoints each team subscribes to. Since this week it takes Swagger 2.0 as it is. This post covers where breaking changes hide in a 2.0 spec, how to get the file out of your build, and what you see once it's connected. Usually nobody chose it. The generator did: Swashbuckle (ASP.NET Core) writes OpenAPI 3.0 by default, but many projects set it to 2.0 (SerializeAsV2 in older versions, OpenApiVersion today) to keep an older client or gateway happy, and never switched back. items.title: A message bus for AI agents in one text file
items.summary: Two AI agent chats working on the same project need a way to talk to each other. Most setups reach for a server, a queue or a database. For a handful of agents on one machine, a text file is enough. This post builds one in about 35 lines of Node, with no packages. The code below was run before it was posted. Every message is one line of JSON appended to a file, bus.ndjson. Each agent remembers how many lines it has already read. That is the whole design. Appending a line is the send. Reading the lines after your cursor is the receive. The file is the history. You can open it and read what your agents said to each other. items.title: Marketplace Avatar Retention: Node.js Signed Object Storage with Deletion Evidence
items.summary: The page fires during a user avatar upload because deletion_eligible_oldest_age has crossed the team's limit. A marketplace seller used a signed object storage write, replaced the avatar, and abandoned another large media transfer; the on-call sees three keys and one uncomfortable question: which bytes can be deleted without breaking a live page or a recovery promise? Short answer: let browsers send large files to object storage with narrowly scoped signed URLs, keep retention decisions in the Node.js SaaS database, and delete only from durable evidence that an object is no longer referenced and its recovery deadline has passed. Proxy uploads through the application only when the application must inspect or transform every byte before accepting it. The transfer path changes capacity. It does not settle ownership. That distinction is the runbook. A direct upload keeps large media off the application's request path, but a completed transfer can outlive the tab that started it. items.title: React Email States: A Typed Fixture Contract
items.summary: Email verification looks like a small React feature: render an input, submit an address, then wait for a message. In a real product, it quickly becomes a state machine. The user can submit twice, the message can arrive late, a test fixture can expire, or the API can return an error after the component has unmounted. The pattern I keep reaching for is a typed UI contract. It gives the component a short list of states and makes impossible combinations harder to represent. That matters for production flows and for test fixtures, where an email inbox may behave like a burner email: useful for a short scenario, but not something the UI should trust forever. A boolean such as isLoading is rarely enough. The screen may need to distinguish between: no address has been submitted yet; a verification request is running; the app is waiting for a matching message; a message was found and accepted; the fixture expired; the user can retry after a temporary failure. If these are represented by several independent booleans, combinations like isLoading: true and hasError: true become possible. items.title: Upgrading .NET Is Easy. Keeping the Business Running Is the Hard Part.
items.summary: What I check before any .NET upgrade, from MVC3 to .NET 10. I shipped my first ASP.NET MVC application on MVC3. Since then I've moved banking platforms, oil & gas field software and several startup products through almost every version of .NET: Framework to Core, Core 3.1 to 6, 6 to 8, and now 8 to 10. The technical side of these upgrades has become much easier over the years. The tooling is better, the migration guides are better, and the framework itself is far more consistent than it used to be. And yet upgrades still go wrong, and in my experience it is rarely because of the framework. It is almost always because of everything around it. This isn't a step-by-step migration guide; Microsoft publishes good ones. It's what I check now, after enough upgrades to know where the pain usually comes from. Every upgrade starts with the same spreadsheet: NuGet packages, target frameworks, and the WCF service nobody wants to touch. That list is necessary, but it is also the least risky part of the job. items.title: Protecting a NestJS API from a flaky AI service with a circuit breaker
items.summary: When your NestJS API depends on an AI service that can be slow or down, every request that waits on it makes the whole API feel broken. In FaceMark, a student attendance system, the NestJS API calls a separate FastAPI service that runs DeepFace/TensorFlow for face recognition. That service is the weakest link, so I put a circuit breaker between the two. Face recognition takes time and sometimes fails. Without protection, a stuck AI service ties up requests in the NestJS API until timeouts pile up, and users see errors on endpoints that have nothing to do with faces. A small circuit breaker class with three states: CLOSED: calls go through. Failures are counted. OPEN: after too many failures, calls fail right away with a clear error. No waiting. HALF_OPEN: after a backoff delay, one trial call is allowed. If it works, the breaker closes. If not, it opens again with a longer delay. The NestJS side wraps the AI call in this breaker, so login, courses and the rest of the API keep working while the AI service recovers. items.title: .NET 8 Is Out of Support: Should You Move to .NET 10 or .NET 11?
items.summary: What changed on 10 November, and how I'd decide as an architect. On 10 November 2026, two things happened on the same day. .NET 8 and .NET 9 reached end of support, and .NET 11 became available. If your systems still run on one of the older versions, the question in your team's chat is probably some version of this: do we move to .NET 10, or skip ahead to .NET 11? For most business systems, my answer is .NET 10. The rest of this post explains why, and when I'd choose differently. According to Microsoft, after 10 November neither .NET 8 nor .NET 9 receives security fixes, servicing updates or technical support. Your applications don't stop working. Nothing breaks on the day. The risk is a quiet one. The next vulnerability found in the runtime or in ASP.NET Core will be fixed in the supported versions only. In regulated environments, an unsupported runtime also tends to show up as an audit finding sooner or later, because the question "are your platforms still receiving security patches?" has a simple answer. items.title: Object Storage Restore Contracts for Node.js Edtech App Data
items.summary: Short answer: define the restore record before choosing the object storage upload path. For an edtech app, a Node.js cron job should publish a database dump and ZIP only after it can identify the tenant, verify the artifact, and prove that the restore request will fetch the exact recorded object. That decision rule came from a familiar production concern: a successful upload is not evidence that a school can recover. Large lesson media should go directly to private object storage so the application does not proxy the bytes, but the application still owns authorization, tenant identity, and recovery state. The first design artifact should be a record that a restore worker can trust. Give each backup a server-generated ID and bind it to the tenant, database dump, selected media set, object key, checksum, schema version, and retention decision. The client must not choose any of those ownership fields. This also separates two workflows that are easy to confuse. A browser may receive a short-lived presigned upload for a large recording. items.title: Dependabot said green. The app was blank. So I made Kane CLI check before it merges
items.summary: Built for the Kane CLI Hackathon by TestMu AI. I found six public repos where the same thing happened. Dependabot opened a React bump. CI went green: type check, lint, build, and in four of them the deploy itself. The PR merged. The live app was a blank page, and the maintainer had to revert it or fix it by hand. One of them put it plainly in the revert: "Format check, lint, typecheck and build stay green, which is why the chain did not catch it." In all six, the bot raised react and left react-dom behind. React refuses to start when the two differ (error #527), so the bundle throws before the first render. Nothing in a normal CI pipeline opens the app, so nothing sees it. Even npm is happy, because react-dom only asks for ^19. A green check on a bot PR means the code builds. It doesn't mean checkout still works. So I built Bumpgate. What it does On every Dependabot or Renovate PR, Bumpgate: builds main and the bump side by side (two git worktrees); has Kane CLI replay your app's critical journeys in a real browser on both; decides with one rule, in plain code: every journey that passes on main must pass on the bump. items.summary: The Associated Press reports: A U.S. jury convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies on Tuesday of conspiring to steal trade secrets and defrauding banks as it grew into one of the world's biggest suppliers of gear for wireless telecommunications networks. But jurors acquitted Huawei of the most serious charge: engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy, a result that the company's lawyer said was a "profound rejection" of the government's narrative that it was corrupt from top to bottom and had a corporate culture of cheating, stealing and lying. Prosecutors had used the charge, commonly found in organized crime and drug cases, to accuse Huawei of operating illicitly to poach intellectual property and technological secrets from competitors and partners. The convictions covered allegations that the company did business in countries subject to U.S. sanctions — including Iran and North Korea — and made false statements to U.S. government officials and banks as part of an effort to hide its misdeeds. Try it on a laptop: https://persona3.rohitpoul.workers.dev A Persona-style menu is the main way you move around About, Resume, Socials and Side Projects each sit behind a menu option Looping background music with CD-player controls Click and selection sound effects Live GitHub stats pulled into the site React, Vite and Framer Motion. Framer Motion handles the animated transitions between menu states and sections, which is most of what makes it feel like a game UI and not a webpage. The Persona menu works because every action has feedback. Moving the cursor, selecting an option and going back each have a visual and an audio response. I tried to keep that. items.summary: 1.What are Custom Hooks in React? They are Javascript functions that allows us to reuse stateful logic between multiple React components. React provides built-in-hooks such as: useState useEffect useContext useReducer we can create our own Hooks based on our requriements. Important rules: A Custom Hook name should start with use. Custom Hooks can use other React Hooks. They help us reuse logic across components. Example of a Custom Hook i import { useState } from "react"; function useCounter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); const increment = () => { setCount(count + 1); }; const decrement = () => { setCount(count - 1); }; return { count, increment, decrement }; } export default useCounter; Here: useCounter is our Custom Hook. useState manages the counter value. increment increases the count. decrement decreases the count. items.title: Turn MacBook Trackpad Into a Speaker - Open Source Swift Tool
items.summary: TL;DR: This tool bypasses standard public haptic limitations by tapping into private macOS frameworks like MultitouchSupport. It takes generated speech, breaks it down into formants every 10 milliseconds, and translates those frequencies into precise sine tones played directly on the trackpad glass. Best for: Mac developers and tinkerers curious about macOS hardware internals and private APIs. Repository snapshot: ⭐ 1 760 stars · 🍴 89 forks · Swift · MIT Daily picks: Follow GitHub Open Source on Telegram nospeaker is a single-file Swift command-line utility that bypasses standard public haptic limitations on macOS. It taps into private frameworks like MultitouchSupport to drive a MacBook or external Magic Trackpad haptic motor at frequencies ranging from 98 Hz to 3,951 Hz, effectively turning the trackpad glass into a miniature speaker. The tool takes generated speech, breaks it down into formants and pitch every 10 milliseconds, and translates those frequencies into precise sine tones. Unvoiced sounds such as s, f, and t are converted into high-tone bursts, which are then played directly on the trackpad glass via rapid motor vibrations. Drives the trackpad motor up to 4,000 times

items.title: I built an app that makes me solve a puzzle before opening social media
items.summary: I kept opening social media "for a second" — and losing 30 minutes. App blockers didn't work for me. One tap to dismiss, and they're off. The reflex was faster than my willpower. So I built Tokokage （やめトコカゲ in Japanese), a small iOS app that inserts one breath of friction: using a Shortcuts personal automation, when you try to open a social app, Tokokage launches first and asks you to clear a tiny puzzle — mini Sudoku, minesweeper, or a slide puzzle. Solve it and the social app opens. But most of the time, that pause is enough to make me think, "Did I actually want to open this?" — and put the phone down. It's deliberately not a hard block. No guilt trips, no locked phone. Just one puzzle between the reflex and the feed. Details: Free, with ads iOS 17 or later Setup: one Shortcuts personal automation per app you want to guard App Store: https://apps.apple.com/app/id6820095179 I originally built it for myself, but if your thumb also opens apps on its own, it might help you too. Feedback welcome — especially which puzzle type works best for you.

items.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has opened an investigation into an Amazon Prime Air delivery drone that struck a fiber-optic cable and crashed onto a residential garage in Michigan after delivering shampoo. The drone lost a propeller and became entangled in power lines, prompting Amazon and local utility workers to coordinate its removal. Amazon offered to help repair the damaged roof and gave the homeowner a $100 gift card. Ars Technica reports: Amazon Prime Air currently operates a fleet of battery-powered MK30 drones that can deliver packages weighing up to five pounds and have onboard sense-and-avoid technology to avoid obstacles. However, the drone clearly failed to avoid the thin fiber-optic cable in this case -- so hopefully the FAA investigation would take that into account along with Amazon delivery drone procedures. It was not clear specifically what information was compromised, but classified material was not jeopardized, the people said. Information at other government agencies was also believed to have been exposed in the breach, according to two of the people. Open-source intelligence can include vast troves of commercially available data sets, social media content, satellite imagery and other online material. Much of it is publicly available, but it can include information sold by data vendors that can be highly revealing, especially when combined with other tranches of data. Spy agencies can also use the data alongside other sources of intelligence to inform analytical judgments.

items.title: I Moved from Coding to Management. Then I Built a Teleprompter to Find My Next Line.
items.summary: I spent years writing code. Then I moved into management, and speaking in front of other people became a much bigger part of my job: team updates, work reports, sharing sessions. I knew the work. I could explain it in writing. But with everyone looking at me, I would get nervous, lose my train of thought, and suddenly forget what came next. That gap surprised me. Experience as a developer had not automatically prepared me to speak confidently about the work. So I approached one small part of the problem in a familiar way: I built a tool. It's called Oralo, a teleprompter that follows my voice. The goal was simple: when I lose my place, help me find the next line. Having a script gives me something to return to. But a teleprompter that scrolls at a fixed speed adds another thing to manage. I don't speak at a fixed speed. I slow down to explain a point. I pause. I add something that wasn't in the draft. When I come back, the text may already have moved on. Now I'm trying to do two things at once: talk to people and find my place on a moving page. items.title: What VP ≠ VNP Means (3 minute read)
items.summary: The Anthropic proof that VP≠VNP means that there is no way to find the permanent of a matrix of 0s and 1s if we are limited to arithmetic circuits of size polynomial in the input-size. This means that for P to equal NP, there must be some trick to computing permanents using AND/OR/NOT on the bits of the input that is better than addition and multiplication. There are many problems where access to Boolean operators is helpful, but it isn't clear how they would help with the permanent. There is a $1 million prize for a solution to this problem.

items.title: Endpoint Security on macOS without the entitlement: eslogger and Swift
items.summary: Endpoint Security is the macOS API that EDR products use to see every process launch, login and permission change. Using it directly requires an entitlement that Apple grants case by case. This post shows how MacSentry, my open-source Mac monitor, gets the same events through /usr/bin/eslogger instead, and what it took to make that fast and quiet: reading JSON Lines without parsing most of them, matching rules against the right program, and not alerting on itself. A native Endpoint Security client needs the com.apple.developer.endpoint-security.client entitlement, and Apple's documentation says plainly that you must request it. For a personal tool built from source, that is not realistic. macOS ships eslogger, a command-line Endpoint Security client that prints events as JSON Lines. MacSentry's helper, macsentry-es, is a root LaunchDaemon that starts eslogger with a list of event names and reads its standard output. The eslogger(1) man page sets the terms, and each one shaped the design: It must run as root, and the responsible process needs Full Disk Access. items.summary: Most AI chat apps send what you type to a server. On recent iPhones there is another option: Apple ships a language model inside iOS, and apps can use it without any network call. Secure AI is an iPhone and iPad app built on that. An iPhone or iPad with iOS 26 and Apple Intelligence. There is nothing to download besides the app, because the model is part of the OS. It is free to download, with in-app purchases. Older devices are not supported. Answers come from the model built into iOS, and a badge on each reply says it ran on device. There is no account to create. The app reads PDFs, scans and photos locally, including text inside pictures. Ask questions about a PDF and get answers that cite the passage they came from. Photograph a receipt and have the items read into a table, then split the bill. Use presets for different kinds of work. Chats are encrypted at rest by iOS. You can lock the app with Face ID, and export backups protected by a passphrase. The built-in model is smaller than the big cloud models, so expect weaker answers on hard reasoning or long, complex documents. The tradeoff is that your questions never leave the phone. items.title: Hackers Compromise Check Point Servers In 22 Organizations
items.summary: Hackers have compromised 24 Check Point Security management servers across 22 organizations in 17 countries in a suspected cyberespionage campaign, according to threat intelligence firm GreyNoise. BleepingComputer reports: The researchers track the activity as GT13 and confirmed it was ongoing between October 17 and November 2, when their visibility ended. However, given the threat actor's persistent access to Check Point devices, they believe the campaign remains active. GreyNoise says the 22 victim organizations are spread across 17 countries, and show no clear evidence of specific targeting. They include government entities, financial services providers, and companies in the energy, transportation, mining, and manufacturing sectors. The attacks were launched from 99 IP addresses that appear to come from compromised Check Point devices and ExpressVPN exit nodes. A Rejetto HTTP File Server, compromised by exploiting CVE-2026-61500, was used as an operational relay for managing intrusions and collecting stolen data from the compromised environments. While GreyNoise could not determine when or how the Check Point servers were breached, it observed the exploitation of CVE-2026-16232

items.title: Recursive Self-Editing: LLMs Program Their Own Weight Edits for Self-Improvement (1 minute read)
items.summary: Today's language models improve themselves through data, training recipes, or scaffolds. Whenever their weights change, gradient descent writes the update, not the model. SELFWRITE lets the model write its own weights. Each generation, the current model studies its own reasoning on fresh training problems, inspects its own weights and activations in a persistent Python session, and writes a program that constructs a low-rank weight edit for itself from white-box primitives. It can raise gate accuracy and accuracy on a held-out test split that the loop never sees without a single gradient step.

items.title: Supercharging transformer residual connections (4 minute read)
items.summary: Google's DeepCrossAttention (DCA) enhances transformer residual connections by allowing each layer to dynamically select and route features from preceding layers, reducing information dilution and parameter count by 30-40%. Unlike traditional residual connections, DCA uses dynamic routing and depth-wise cross-attention mechanisms to achieve faster convergence and better quality with minimal parameter increase. Tested on large datasets like C4 and LM1B, DCA improves training efficiency and perplexity compared to standard models, proving a shift towards dynamic residual routing for scalable LLMs.

items.title: AI x Bio is not _just_ a data problem (14 minute read)
items.summary: How far AI gets in biology will depend largely on how much data we have. It will also depend on what is measured and the quality of that data. An abundance of systematically incomplete measurements is unlikely to lead to a comprehensive understanding of many of the complex systems that occur in biology. AI will likely become a powerful tool that will contribute to the study of biology, but there is still no clear path to documenting a comprehensive account of how a whole cell or tissue works.
